title: Window Magic — Window Functions & Recursive CTEs

subChunks.title: Window Functions — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD
subChunks.hookHtml: GROUP BY collapses rows. Window functions compute per-row values that look across multiple rows — without collapsing. "Rank each apprentice by XP within their cohort", "the previous quest's completion time", "a running total" — none of these can be done with GROUP BY alone. Window functions are the single biggest analytics tool in modern SQL.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The mental shift

GROUP BY: many rows in, fewer rows out. Each output row is a summary of one bucket.

Window function: many rows in, same number of rows out. Each output row keeps its original values plus one extra computed across a "window" of related rows.

-- GROUP BY — collapses to one row per rank:
SELECT rank, AVG(xp) FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank;

-- Window function — keeps every row, adds an avg-per-rank column:
SELECT name, rank, xp,
       AVG(xp) OVER (PARTITION BY rank) AS avg_in_rank
FROM apprentices;

Both compute a per-rank average. GROUP BY gives you 4 rows (one per rank); the window form gives you all 4 apprentices, each with their rank's average alongside.

Anatomy of a window function

function() OVER (
  PARTITION BY column1, column2     -- which rows form one window
  ORDER BY     column3 DESC          -- ordering within the window
  ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW   -- frame within the ordering
)

Three parts in the OVER clause:

  • PARTITION BY — splits rows into independent windows. Optional; if omitted, the whole result set is one window.
  • ORDER BY — orders rows within each window. Required for ranking, lag/lead, and running totals.
  • ROWS / RANGE — narrows the window to a frame relative to the current row (e.g. "the last 3 rows"). Optional.

The four families of window functions

1. Ranking — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK

SELECT name, rank, xp,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC) AS dense_rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC) AS dense
FROM apprentices;

Differences when there are ties:

  • ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3, 4 — always sequential, ties broken arbitrarily
  • RANK: 1, 2, 2, 4 — ties share a rank, then the next value skips
  • DENSE_RANK: 1, 2, 2, 3 — ties share, no skip

For "top-N per group" — the canonical use case — you want ROW_NUMBER:

-- Top 1 quest by xp_reward in each difficulty tier:
SELECT difficulty, title
FROM (
  SELECT difficulty, title,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY difficulty
                            ORDER BY xp_reward DESC) AS rn
  FROM quests
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

2. Aggregates — over a window

Every aggregate (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) can be a window function:

SELECT name, xp,
       SUM(xp) OVER ()                      AS total_xp,        -- whole table
       AVG(xp) OVER (PARTITION BY rank)     AS avg_in_rank,     -- per rank
       COUNT(*) OVER ()                     AS num_apprentices  -- whole table
FROM apprentices;

Most useful when you need a per-row value relative to the whole or to a partition — "this apprentice's xp as a percentage of total xp."

3. Running totals — frames

-- Cumulative completions over time:
SELECT date,
       count_today,
       SUM(count_today) OVER (
         ORDER BY date
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_total
FROM daily_completions
ORDER BY date;

The frame ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW says "sum from the first row up to and including this one." Other frames: 3 PRECEDING for a moving 3-row average, UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING for a backwards-looking total.

4. Offsets — LAG and LEAD

-- Each completion alongside the previous one (per apprentice):
SELECT apprentice_id, completed_at,
       LAG(completed_at)  OVER (PARTITION BY apprentice_id
                                 ORDER BY completed_at) AS prev_at,
       LEAD(completed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY apprentice_id
                                 ORDER BY completed_at) AS next_at
FROM completions;

LAG(col) reads the value of col in the previous row in the window. LEAD(col) reads the next row. The most common use: computing differences between consecutive events without a self-join. "Time between this completion and the previous one" was historically a self-join nightmare; with LAG it's one line.

Where window functions can appear

Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING — but before ORDER BY and LIMIT. They live in the SELECT list and (in some engines) the ORDER BY clause. You cannot reference a window function in a WHERE clause directly — you must wrap the query in a CTE or subquery and filter on the result:

-- ERROR — window functions can't be in WHERE:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY xp DESC) <= 3;

-- Wrap in a CTE:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY xp DESC) AS rn
  FROM apprentices
)
SELECT name FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

Why window functions matter

Before window functions (added to the SQL standard in 2003, widely implemented by 2010), "top N per group" required either an ugly correlated subquery or a self-join. Both were slow on big data and error-prone to write. With window functions, the same query is one PARTITION BY clause. Almost every analytics dashboard, leaderboard, or per-group report you'll write in your career uses them. Master ROW_NUMBER, then RANK, then LAG/LEAD — those three cover 90% of cases.

storyBeats.text: Cipher slides a fresh sheet across the desk and draws a column of names with a number beside each — like a leaderboard.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: GROUP BY collapses. If you want "the average XP per rank", GROUP BY gives you four rows. But what if you want every apprentice plus their rank's average alongside — same row count, extra column? GROUP BY cannot help. Window functions can. Same input, same row count, plus computed values that look across nearby rows.

storyBeats.speaker: GROUP BY vs window — the same average
storyBeats.text:
-- GROUP BY collapses to one row per rank:
SELECT rank, AVG(xp) AS mean_xp
FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank;
-- 4 rows.

-- Window: same average, alongside every apprentice:
SELECT name, rank, xp,
       AVG(xp) OVER (PARTITION BY rank) AS mean_xp
FROM apprentices;
-- 4 rows — but you can also see each apprentice's individual XP
-- and their rank's average in the same row. Useful for things like
-- 'how does each apprentice compare to the average for their rank?'.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The OVER clause has three parts. PARTITION BY defines independent windows — like running the function once per rank, separately. ORDER BY orders the rows within each window — required for ranking and for LAG/LEAD. The optional ROWS BETWEEN ... frame narrows the window to a specific range of rows around the current one — for moving averages, running totals, that kind of thing.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Four families. Ranking — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK — for leaderboards and top-N-per-group. Aggregates — SUM, AVG, COUNT — for per-row-versus-total comparisons. Running totals — same aggregates with a frame. Offsets — LAG and LEAD — for looking at the previous or next row. Master ROW_NUMBER first; it shows up in every analytics interview.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And one trap: you cannot use a window function directly in WHERE. Window functions run after WHERE evaluates. To filter on a window result — like "only the top 3 per rank" — you wrap the SELECT in a CTE, then filter the CTE. WITH ranked AS (... ROW_NUMBER() OVER ...) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3. The pattern is so common it has a name: 'top-N per group'.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Top per rank — the canonical window query

Cipher wants the highest-XP apprentice in each rank — one row per rank, with the apprentice's name and XP. This is the canonical "top-N per group" pattern: ROW_NUMBER inside a CTE, then filter on rn = 1 outside.

  • Three columns: rank, name, xp
  • Inside a CTE, compute ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC)
  • In the outer query, filter where the row number equals 1

Reference data:

id | name    | rank        | xp
---+---------+-------------+------
 1 | Alice   | Apprentice  | 1200
 2 | Bjorn   | Adept       | 2400
 3 | Cassia  | Mage        | 4800
 4 | Dorian  | Novice      |   80
 5 | Eleanor | Apprentice  | 1500

Expected 4 rows: Apprentice/Eleanor/1500, Adept/Bjorn/2400, Mage/Cassia/4800, Novice/Dorian/80. (Apprentice has two — Eleanor wins because she has higher XP.)
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Top apprentice per rank, using ROW_NUMBER + a CTE.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, rank, xp,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           -- PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY xp DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM apprentices
)
SELECT rank, name, xp
FROM ranked
WHERE
  -- rn = 1
;

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo Challenge — The XP gap to the next apprentice

Same data. Write a query that returns each apprentice and their XP, alongside the XP of the next apprentice down the leaderboard. Use LEAD(xp) OVER (ORDER BY xp DESC). Columns: name, xp, next_xp. The lowest-XP apprentice will have NULL for next_xp.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between GROUP BY and a window function with PARTITION BY. Use the apprentices table to give an example where you want both the per-rank average AND every apprentice's individual row — and explain why this requires a window function rather than GROUP BY.

questions.questionHtml: What's the key difference between GROUP BY and a window function?
options: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group; a window function keeps every row and adds a per-row computed value
Window functions can only do COUNT and SUM
GROUP BY is faster than window functions in every case
Window functions don't take an aggregate
questions.correctAnswer: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group; a window function keeps every row and adds a per-row computed value
questions.explanationHtml: GROUP BY: many rows in, fewer rows out. Window function: many rows in, same number of rows out. The window function computes its value across a window of related rows but keeps the row count unchanged. This is precisely why window functions enabled "top-N per group" without self-joins or correlated subqueries.

questions.questionHtml:
Using the five-apprentice table from the lesson, what does this query return for the row where Bjorn appears?

SELECT name, rank, xp,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC) AS rn
FROM apprentices;
options: Bjorn, Adept, 2400, 1 — he's the only Adept, so he's #1 in his partition
Bjorn, Adept, 2400, 2 — he's the second-highest XP overall
Bjorn, Adept, 2400, 5 — there are 5 apprentices
Bjorn, Adept, 2400, NULL — partitions can't have a single row
questions.correctAnswer: Bjorn, Adept, 2400, 1 — he's the only Adept, so he's #1 in his partition
questions.explanationHtml: PARTITION BY rank creates four windows — Apprentice (Alice, Eleanor), Adept (Bjorn), Mage (Cassia), Novice (Dorian). Within each window, ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3, … by ORDER BY xp DESC. Bjorn is alone in Adept, so he's rn=1.

questions.questionHtml: You want "the second-highest XP apprentice in each rank." Which approach is correct?
options: WITH ranked AS (SELECT name, rank, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC) AS rn FROM apprentices) SELECT name, rank FROM ranked WHERE rn = 2;
SELECT name, rank FROM apprentices WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC) = 2;
SELECT name, rank FROM apprentices ORDER BY xp DESC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1;
SELECT name, rank, AVG(xp) FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank HAVING xp = 'second';
questions.correctAnswer: WITH ranked AS (SELECT name, rank, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rank ORDER BY xp DESC) AS rn FROM apprentices) SELECT name, rank FROM ranked WHERE rn = 2;
questions.explanationHtml: The CTE-then-filter pattern. Window functions cannot appear directly in WHERE because WHERE runs before window evaluation. Wrap the windowed SELECT in a CTE, then filter on the result. Option 2 is the syntactically illegal version. Option 3 is global top-2 with offset, not per-rank. Option 4 is invalid SQL.

questions.questionHtml: You're computing "time between consecutive completions for each apprentice." Which approach is the most idiomatic and efficient?
options: LAG(completed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY apprentice_id ORDER BY completed_at) — computes the previous completion in one pass, no self-join
Self-join completions to itself, matching each row to the row with the next-smaller completed_at — works but requires careful row matching and is slow on big tables
Use a correlated subquery for each row to find the previous completion
Order by completed_at and read consecutive rows in application code
questions.correctAnswer: LAG(completed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY apprentice_id ORDER BY completed_at) — computes the previous completion in one pass, no self-join
questions.explanationHtml: LAG is the canonical solution for "compare each row to the previous." One pass through the data, no self-join, no correlated subquery. The other approaches all work in principle but are dramatically slower and harder to read. Before window functions, the self-join pattern was the standard — and queries that took seconds with LAG took minutes without it.

subChunks.title: Recursive CTEs — Walking Trees and Graphs
subChunks.hookHtml: SQL is famously bad at hierarchical data. "Find every descendant of this node", "the chain of managers above this employee", "the tree of dependent tasks" — none of these have a fixed depth, so a fixed number of joins won't work. Recursive CTEs are how SQL handles unbounded hierarchies in a single query. They're rarely needed — but when they are, nothing else will do.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The shape of a recursive CTE

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  -- Base case: where do we start?
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees
  WHERE id = 17

  UNION ALL

  -- Recursive case: how do we extend by one step?
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT * FROM chain ORDER BY depth;

Two parts joined by UNION ALL:

  • Anchor / base — the starting rows. Often a single row by id.
  • Recursive step — produce the next layer of rows by joining the CTE to itself (the running result of all prior steps).

The engine evaluates the anchor, gets some rows, then re-runs the recursive step using those rows as input, accumulating new rows each pass. It stops when a recursive iteration produces zero new rows.

The classic use case — organisational hierarchy

-- employees(id PK, name, manager_id FK -> employees.id)
-- Find every employee under id=1, with their depth in the tree:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees
  WHERE id = 1                                    -- start at the boss

  UNION ALL

  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org      o ON e.manager_id = o.id          -- direct reports
)
SELECT name, depth FROM org ORDER BY depth, name;

The reverse direction — chain to the top

-- Walk upward from a leaf to the root:
WITH RECURSIVE upline AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id
  FROM employees
  WHERE id = 42                                   -- start at the leaf

  UNION ALL

  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id
  FROM employees e
  JOIN upline u ON u.manager_id = e.id            -- step one level up
)
SELECT * FROM upline;

Same shape, different join direction. Down the tree: join on "my parent is in the running set." Up the tree: join on "my id is the parent of someone in the running set."

Generating sequences — recursion without a table

-- Numbers 1 to 10, no source table:
WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (
  SELECT 1 AS n
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 10
)
SELECT * FROM nums;

Sometimes useful for filling date gaps, generating test rows, or producing a calendar table.

The cycle problem

If your data has cycles — A reports to B, B reports to A — a naive recursive CTE will loop forever. Most engines have safeguards (PostgreSQL has a recursion depth limit; SQL Server requires OPTION (MAXRECURSION ...)) but the proper fix is to detect the cycle in your query:

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, ARRAY[id] AS path
  FROM employees WHERE id = 17

  UNION ALL

  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, path || e.id
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
  WHERE NOT (e.id = ANY(c.path))                  -- stop if seen before
)
SELECT * FROM chain;

Carry an array of visited ids; refuse to revisit. Engine-specific syntax — PostgreSQL uses arrays; SQL Server uses STRING_AGG paths; check your manual.

When NOT to use recursive CTEs

Recursive CTEs are powerful but slow on big data. If you're walking a hierarchy thousands of times a day, consider:

  • Materialised path — store each row's path-from-root as a string ("1.7.42"). Find descendants with WHERE path LIKE '1.7.%'.
  • Closure table — a separate table with one row per (ancestor, descendant) pair. Lookups are O(1).
  • Nested sets — left/right numbering scheme. Fast reads, expensive writes.

Each scheme trades query speed for write complexity. For occasional hierarchical queries, recursive CTEs are fine. For hot paths, consider one of the alternatives.

The mental model

Picture the recursive step as a loop in your head:

// Pseudocode for the descendants query:
result = []
current_layer = [employee 17]
while current_layer not empty:
    result.extend(current_layer)
    current_layer = direct_reports_of(current_layer)
return result

The recursive CTE is exactly that loop, expressed declaratively. The anchor is the initial layer. The recursive step is "compute the next layer from the current." UNION ALL accumulates the layers. Termination is implicit — when the next layer is empty, the loop stops.

storyBeats.text: Cipher walks you to a section of the Hall you have not seen before — a tall column of slim ledgers, each linking to the one above and below.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Some questions cannot be answered by joins of fixed depth. 'Every apprentice descended from this mentor — at any depth.' 'The chain of mentors above this apprentice — until we reach the Archmage.' These are hierarchical queries. They walk a tree until they reach the leaves or the root. JOIN cannot do that — JOIN has fixed depth at parse time.

storyBeats.speaker: A recursive CTE — descendants
storyBeats.text:
-- mentors(id, name, mentor_id) — each apprentice has one mentor.
-- Find everyone descended from mentor id=1:

WITH RECURSIVE descendants AS (
  -- Anchor: mentor 1 themselves.
  SELECT id, name, mentor_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM mentors
  WHERE id = 1

  UNION ALL

  -- Recursive step: join the running set to its direct apprentices.
  SELECT m.id, m.name, m.mentor_id, d.depth + 1
  FROM mentors m
  JOIN descendants d ON m.mentor_id = d.id
)
SELECT name, depth FROM descendants ORDER BY depth, name;

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Two parts, joined by UNION ALL. The anchor says where to start. The recursive step says how to extend by one level — by joining the CTE to itself. The engine runs the anchor, accumulates the result, then runs the recursive step using the latest results, and so on. It stops when a step produces no new rows.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And one warning: cycles. If A's mentor is B, and B's mentor is A, a naive recursive CTE loops forever. Most engines have a recursion limit that catches this — PostgreSQL by default, SQL Server with OPTION (MAXRECURSION). But the proper fix is to detect the cycle in your query. Carry an array of visited ids; refuse to revisit. Production hierarchies sometimes do have cycles, especially in legacy data — defend against them.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Recursive CTEs are powerful but they are not free. Each iteration is a join. A 10-deep hierarchy is 10 joins. For occasional hierarchical queries, this is fine. For hot paths — say, every web request loads the full org chart — consider materialised paths or closure tables, where the hierarchy is precomputed and queries are flat lookups. The engineering trade-off is read speed vs write complexity. Recursive CTEs are the right tool for read-light, write-heavy hierarchical data.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Trace each recursion

For each query, identify the anchor (the starting rows) and the recursive step (how each pass extends the result). Predict the final row count for the given data.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- mentors(id, name, mentor_id):
-- 1=Solomon (root, mentor_id=NULL)
-- 2=Cipher (mentor_id=1)
-- 3=Lyra (mentor_id=1)
-- 4=Vex (mentor_id=2)
-- 5=Wren (mentor_id=2)
-- 6=Yara (mentor_id=4)

-- Query A — every descendant of Solomon:
WITH RECURSIVE descendants AS (
  SELECT id, name, mentor_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM mentors WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT m.id, m.name, m.mentor_id, d.depth + 1
  FROM mentors m
  JOIN descendants d ON m.mentor_id = d.id
)
SELECT name, depth FROM descendants ORDER BY depth, name;
-- Result: Solomon(1), Cipher(2), Lyra(2), Vex(3), Wren(3), Yara(4)

-- Query B — chain upward from Yara to root:
WITH RECURSIVE upline AS (
  SELECT id, name, mentor_id
  FROM mentors WHERE id = 6
  UNION ALL
  SELECT m.id, m.name, m.mentor_id
  FROM mentors m
  JOIN upline u ON u.mentor_id = m.id
)
SELECT name FROM upline;
-- Result: Yara, Vex, Cipher, Solomon

-- Query C — generate numbers 1 to 5 (no source table):
WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (
  SELECT 1 AS n
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5
)
SELECT n FROM nums;
-- Result: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk a junior through a recursive CTE that finds every descendant of a node in an organisational hierarchy. Identify the anchor and the recursive step, and explain how the engine knows when to stop.

questions.questionHtml: What two parts make up a recursive CTE?
options: The anchor (base case) and the recursive step, joined by UNION ALL
The SELECT and the FROM
The PARTITION BY and the ORDER BY
The BEGIN and the COMMIT
questions.correctAnswer: The anchor (base case) and the recursive step, joined by UNION ALL
questions.explanationHtml: Anchor = the starting rows. Recursive step = how to extend by one level by joining the CTE to itself. UNION ALL accumulates layers. Termination: when the recursive step produces zero new rows, the engine stops.

questions.questionHtml: Using the mentor hierarchy from the lesson (Solomon → Cipher, Lyra; Cipher → Vex, Wren; Vex → Yara), how many rows does the descendants-of-Solomon query return?
options: 6 — Solomon and all 5 descendants
5 — every descendant excluding Solomon
3 — only direct reports of Solomon
1 — only Solomon
questions.explanationHtml: Anchor: Solomon (1 row, depth 1). Step 1: Cipher, Lyra (depth 2). Step 2: Vex, Wren (depth 3, both report to Cipher). Step 3: Yara (depth 4, reports to Vex). Step 4: nothing new — termination. Total: 6 rows.

questions.questionHtml: What goes wrong with a naive recursive CTE if the data contains a cycle (A's mentor is B, B's mentor is A)?
options: The recursion never terminates because each step keeps producing new rows; most engines have a recursion-depth safeguard, but the proper fix is to track visited ids and skip them
The query returns NULL
The query returns the cycle in a single row
The query is automatically rewritten as iterative
questions.correctAnswer: The recursion never terminates because each step keeps producing new rows; most engines have a recursion-depth safeguard, but the proper fix is to track visited ids and skip them
questions.explanationHtml: Cycles cause infinite recursion. PostgreSQL has a recursion limit (configurable); SQL Server requires OPTION (MAXRECURSION). The safeguard prevents runaway queries, but the underlying data is still problematic. The fix: carry an array of visited ids in the recursive step and add WHERE NOT (e.id = ANY(path)) to refuse revisits. Some real-world hierarchies have cycles by accident (legacy data, bugs), so defending against them is good practice.

questions.questionHtml: Your application loads the full org chart on every web request and walks it with a recursive CTE. Performance is poor — each request takes 200ms in the database. What's the most appropriate fix?
options: Switch to a precomputed structure like a closure table or materialised path; recursive CTEs are read-light/write-heavy and not optimal for hot read paths
Add an index on every column of the employees table
Replace the recursive CTE with a non-recursive CTE
Use SELECT * to ensure all columns are read at once
questions.correctAnswer: Switch to a precomputed structure like a closure table or materialised path; recursive CTEs are read-light/write-heavy and not optimal for hot read paths
questions.explanationHtml: Recursive CTEs do real work on every query — N joins for an N-level hierarchy. For occasional hierarchical queries this is fine; for high-frequency reads it's not. The standard solutions: (a) materialised path: store each row's path-from-root as a string "1.7.42", find descendants with LIKE; (b) closure table: a separate table with one row per (ancestor, descendant) pair, lookups are O(1). Both add write complexity (every hierarchy change must update the precomputed structure) but make reads instant. Indexing every column is a wasteful response. Non-recursive CTEs can't express hierarchical traversal.
